title: Lending your money
blurb: Savings accounts, GICs, T-bills and bonds, and why bond prices move.

levels.title: Four ways to lend
learn: Name the four common ways to lend money.
Say who you lend to, for how long, and how you are paid.

cards.text: Lending means letting someone else use your money for a while. They promise to pay it back, and they pay you for the loan. Four common ways to lend are a savings account, a GIC, a T-bill and a bond. Each one answers three questions: who, for how long, and how you get paid.
The table puts the four side by side. Read across a row to see who you lend to, for how long, and how you are paid. The next cards take them one at a time.

figure.title: Four ways to lend
rows: You pay less, get face value
A coupon each year, then face value

cards.text: A savings account and a GIC are both loans to a bank. You can take money out of a savings account at any time with no penalty. A GIC runs for a set term and is locked in. In this example, $2,500.00 in a GIC at 3% earns $75.00 in one year.

A T-bill is a short loan to a government, such as for 3 months. It pays no interest. You buy it for less than its face value, here $1,000.00, and you get the full face value back at the end. Your gain is the gap. Buy at $985.00 and you gain $15.00.

A bond is a loan to a government or a company for a number of years. It pays a coupon, a fixed payment, once a year in these examples. At the end, the maturity, you get the face value back. A $1,000.00 bond with a 4% coupon pays $40.00 a year for its years, then returns the $1,000.00.

A bond can be sold to another buyer before it ends. A debenture is a company bond backed only by the company’s promise to pay, with no asset behind it. Level 2 asks how safe each way is. Level 3 asks what a bond sells for.

levels.title: Safe, locked or both
learn: Say why a riskier borrower pays a higher rate.
Say what deposit insurance and a GIC do and do not cover.

cards.text: Lenders ask for more when a borrower is more likely not to pay back. A government is among the safest to lend to. A new business with no sales history is among the riskiest. The rate is the price of the risk: the riskier the borrower, the higher the rate asked.

If a bank fails, deposit insurance helps you get your deposit back, up to a limit. In Canada, CDIC is the deposit insurer for banks. The limit and what is covered can change, so check the insurer’s own website. A credit union has its own insurer, so check that one. A bond is not a deposit.

A GIC is guaranteed, but guaranteed does not mean no risk. The guarantee is your principal and the stated rate, in dollars, for the set term. It does not promise that the rate beats rising prices. It does not promise you will not miss a better rate. It does not let you out early.

Mina puts $1,000.00 in a 5-year GIC at 4%. It pays $40.00 a year. A year later, new GICs pay 6%, which would be $60.00 a year. Her GIC has no price that can fall, but she cannot leave. She is locked in at 4% while the market pays 6%, which is $20.00 a year less.

Cash is money you can spend now. A cash equivalent is a very safe, short-term place that turns into cash fast, such as a savings account or a short T-bill. A five-year GIC is grouped with cash but is slow to get out of: not a true cash equivalent. Safety and how fast you can get out are two different questions.

In the Net Worth building you can hold a savings account and buy a GIC for 12, 36 or 60 months, from $100.00. Savings money is there at any time. A GIC is locked: you cannot take it out early. The game starts the savings rate at 2.75% a year. It can change, so read the live rate there.

levels.title: Why bond prices move
learn: Say which way a bond’s price moves when rates change.
Work out a one-year bond price and read the five-year example.

cards.text: A bond does not have to be held to the end. Its owner can sell it to another buyer. What a buyer will pay depends on what new bonds pay today, the market yield. Ayo owns a 5-year bond with a $1,000.00 face value and a 4% coupon: $40.00 a year.

Rates rise to 6%. A new $1,000.00 bond now pays $60.00 a year. No one pays $1,000.00 for Ayo’s $40.00 a year when $60.00 is on offer. So the price of his bond falls below face value, a discount. If rates fall, the price rises above face value, a premium.

A price is what the payments are worth today. A payment is worth less today than when it arrives, because you could earn the market yield while you wait. Divide it by 1.06 for each year, at 6%. Coupons here come once a year. A 1-year bond pays $1,040.00: $1,040.00 / 1.06 = $981.13.

For the 5-year bond, divide each coupon by 1.06 for as many years as it waits, and do the same for the $1,000.00 at the end. Add up what they are worth today. The class example gives $915.75. That is $84.25 below face value.

figure.title: The 5-year bond at a 6% market yield

cards.text: A longer bond swings more. A 10-year bond with the same 4% coupon has a price of $852.80 at a 6% market yield, against $915.75 for the 5-year one. More years of the low coupon means a bigger fall. A longer bond is riskier if you must sell it.

If Ayo holds the bond to the end, he gets all five coupons and the face value back, whatever the price did. The fall hurts only if he has to sell early. A GIC has no price that falls, but it cannot be sold, so it is locked in at its rate. A bond shows its price every day.
